summary: Gives a framework and service-level requirements for Layer 1 Virtual Private Networks, where a provider offers customers private connectivity over its lower-level transport network. It covers why such services are wanted, what they must provide, and some architectural models for building them. It is informational and guides later protocol work.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4847 describes how a provider can offer customers restricted layer-1 connections between their sites. It sets out service models and requirements for how customers request connections and what information the provider shares.

subtitle: A framework for private layer-1 connectivity over a provider network.

tldr.problem: Customers may want layer-1 connections between their sites without building and managing a full transport network. Providers need service models that limit connectivity and control what network information customers can see.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4847 defines an L1VPN framework, service-level requirements, and several service models. These models vary in signaling, routing information shared with customers, and whether provider resources are shared or dedicated.
tldr.outcome: The Informational framework is intended to guide interoperable L1VPN protocols and mechanisms. It does not define a complete protocol solution.

sections.title: What a Layer 1 VPN Provides
sections.content:
A Layer 1 VPN (L1VPN) is a provider service that supplies layer-1 connectivity between two or more customer sites, while giving the customer some control over establishing the connection and its type. Layer-1 networks include spatial, wavelength, and time-division switching.

The framework considers networks controlled with GMPLS. A provider network has Provider Edge (PE) devices at customer connections and Provider (P) devices in its core; Customer Edge (CE) devices connect customer sites. A VPN connection joins CE endpoints that belong to the same VPN.
sections.plainLanguage: An L1VPN gives a customer connections between selected sites through a provider's transport network. The provider controls the core, while the service model determines how much control and information the customer receives.

sections.title: Why Customers and Providers Use L1VPNs
sections.content:
A customer can outsource management of layer-1 connectivity and use part of a shared network instead of bearing the cost of deploying and managing one. A provider can offer on-demand services and make more flexible use of spare network resources.

The RFC describes scenarios including a carrier's internal multi-service backbone, one carrier buying service from another, resource trading among providers, connections across administrative domains, and scheduled connections. Inter-AS and inter-provider L1VPNs require further analysis beyond this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers can request connectivity without operating the provider's transport network themselves. Providers can share resources among services, while keeping each customer's permitted connections separate.

sections.title: Service Models and Customer Visibility
sections.content:
The management-based model lets customer and provider management systems request and manage connections; it has no CE-to-PE control-message exchange. The basic signaling model lets a CE request a connection through the provider but does not give it routing information about remote customer sites or the provider network.

The enhanced signaling-and-routing model adds limited exchange of customer reachability or traffic-engineering information. Its variants include Overlay Extension, Virtual Node, Virtual Link, and Per-VPN Peer. The models differ in what the customer can see and whether provider data-plane resources are shared or dedicated to a VPN.
sections.plainLanguage: Some customers request connections through provider management systems. Other models let customer equipment signal directly, and the enhanced models share selected routing information to support customer path planning.

sections.title: Service, Recovery and Security Requirements
sections.content:
The framework calls for accounting information for each VPN and secure communication between customer and provider. Unnecessary information, especially information about other VPNs, must not be exposed. The provider should support fault, configuration, accounting, and performance management.

Recovery may cover the provider's PE-to-PE portion, customer-to-provider links, or the full CE-to-CE connection, and these scopes may be combined. Security requirements include integrity, confidentiality, mutual authentication, access control, and protection against denial-of-service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers need information about their own service, not other VPNs. The provider must protect management exchanges and control who can request connections or see network information.
